title: Matching rows across tables
objectives: Join two tables with an inner join on a key
Predict the row count of a join, and spot one that multiplies rows
Chain three tables and read a query plan

screens.title: Which close goes with which trade?
screens.prose: Trades 1 and 4 are both in Barclays, on different days. To value a trade we need the close of its stock on the day it was done.
screens.question: Tap the close that values trade 1 and the close that values trade 4.

hints.text: On which date was each Barclays trade done?
Trade 1 was on 2 March and trade 4 on 3 March.
Tap the BARC close for 2026-03-02 and the BARC close for 2026-03-03.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each trade on both its ticker and its date.

byKey.ticker-only: You matched on the ticker alone. Each trade happened on one day, so it needs that day's close only.
byKey.r2c2: That is the 4 March close. Neither Barclays trade happened that day.
byKey.r3c2: That is a Shell close. Trades 1 and 4 are in BARC.
byKey.r4c2: That is a Shell close. Trades 1 and 4 are in BARC.
byKey.r5c2: That is a Shell close. Trades 1 and 4 are in BARC.
byKey.r0c2: You missed trade 1, done on 2 March.
byKey.r1c2: You missed trade 4, done on 3 March.

explain.text: Each trade met the price row with the same ticker and the same date. Pairing rows across two tables like this is a **join**. SQL writes the matching rule after the word `ON`.

screens.title: JOIN ... ON
screens.prose:
SQL can do the matching. `JOIN ... ON` pairs each row on the left with every row on the right where `ON` is true. `t` and `s` are short names for the tables.

```sql
SELECT t.id, s.name
FROM trades AS t
JOIN securities AS s
  ON t.ticker = s.ticker;
```
screens.question: How many rows does it return?

hints.text: How many companies can one trade's ticker match?
Every ticker appears once in `securities`.
Each of the 7 trades finds exactly one company, so there is one row per trade.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many companies each trade matches.

byKey.companies: That is the number of companies. Each trade finds one company, so there is one row per trade.
byKey.cross: That is every trade paired with every company. `ON` keeps only the pairs with the same ticker.
byKey.distinct: Barclays and Shell are traded twice each, and each trade keeps its own row.

explain.text: Each trade's ticker matches one company, because `ticker` is the primary key of `securities`. So the join gives one row per trade: 7. This is an **inner join**: only pairs that satisfy `ON` survive.

screens.title: Half a key
screens.prose:
Now join trades to prices to fetch each trade's close. A first attempt matches on the ticker only. Every ticker has three closes in `prices`.

```sql
SELECT t.id, p.date, p.close
FROM trades AS t
JOIN prices AS p
  ON t.ticker = p.ticker;
```
screens.question: How many rows does it return?

widget.label: Rows returned
widget.accept: 21: each of the 7 trades pairs with 3 closes.

hints.text: How many BARC rows does trade 1 meet?
Trade 1 matches all three BARC closes, not just one.
Each of the 7 trades matches 3 closes: $7 \times 3$.

feedback.correct: Seven trades times three closes each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the closes one trade matches, then multiply.

byKey.one-each: You expected one close per trade. With only the ticker in `ON`, trade 1 matches all three BARC closes.
byKey.prices: That is the number of price rows. Each trade pairs with the three closes of its stock: $7 \times 3$.
byKey.cross: That would be every trade with every price. `ON` still requires the tickers to match.

explain.text: `ticker` is only half of the key of `prices`. Each trade matches all three closes of its stock, so 7 trades become $7 \times 3 = 21$ rows. A sum of trade values over this result would be three times too big.

screens.title: The missing ON
screens.prose:
A colleague counts the rows of a join but forgets the `ON` line:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM trades
JOIN securities;
```
screens.question: What does SQLite return?

options.why: You expected SQL to match the tickers by itself. It never guesses: with no `ON`, every pair of rows is kept.
You added the row counts. A join pairs rows, so the counts multiply: $7 \times 6$.
SQLite accepts a join with no `ON` and keeps every pair. That is why the slip is easy to miss.

hints.text: Without `ON`, which pairs of rows are kept?
Trade 1 pairs with all six companies, and so does every other trade.
7 trades, each paired with 6 companies: $7 \times 6$.

feedback.correct: Every trade with every company: 42 rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no condition, which pairs survive?

byKey.seven: You expected SQL to match the tickers on its own. With no `ON`, it keeps every pair of rows.

explain.text: With no `ON`, every trade pairs with every company: $7 \times 6 = 42$ rows. This is a **cross join**, and any sum over it is inflated. Compare the row count with what you expect after every join.

screens.title: The whole key
screens.prose: Back to trades and prices. The primary key of `prices` is the pair `(ticker, date)`.
screens.question: Which `ON` gives exactly one close per trade?

options.why: You joined on the date alone. Each trade then pairs with all six closes of its day: 42 rows.
That is half the key. Each trade pairs with three closes: 21 rows.
You joined on the wrong column. A trade id is a number and never equals a ticker, so no rows come back.

hints.text: Which columns make up the key of `prices`?
One close is fixed by a ticker and a date together.
Name both key columns in `ON`, joined with `AND`.

feedback.correct: Both key columns: one close per trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `ON` must name the whole key of `prices`.

explain.text: The key of `prices` is `(ticker, date)`, so `ON` names both columns. Each trade then meets exactly one close, and the join keeps 7 rows.

screens.title: Three tables
screens.prose: Joins chain: each `JOIN` adds one table with its own `ON`. Value every trade at that day's close: the quantity times the close, in pounds. A sale has a negative quantity, so its value is negative.
screens.question: Return `id`, `name` and `ROUND(qty * close, 2)` for every trade, sorted by id.

screens.title: Reading a query plan
screens.prose: A real `prices` table, with no key declared, holds 2,000 tickers over five years: 2,520,000 rows. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows how SQLite will find BP's closes. Without an index it plans a `SCAN`. After `CREATE INDEX idx_ticker ON prices (ticker)` it plans a `SEARCH`.
screens.question: About how many rows does each plan read to find BP's closes?

options.why: An index is a sorted list of tickers with row positions. The search jumps to BP's rows and skips the rest.
BP has one close per day for five years, so 1,260 rows match. The index finds all of them.
A scan cannot stop early. BP's rows could be anywhere, so it reads every row.

hints.text: What does a scan do with each row?
A scan reads every row; a search through an index reads only the matches.
BP has 1,260 closes, one per day for five years. The scan reads all 2,520,000 rows.

feedback.correct: The scan reads everything; the search reads only BP.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which plan reads every row?

explain.text: `SCAN` reads every row; `SEARCH ... USING INDEX` jumps straight to the matches. A join does one lookup per trade, so an index on the join key turns millions of reads into thousands. A primary key gets an index automatically.

screens.title: The join pattern
screens.prose:
You matched rows on the whole key, then chained a third table. When each `ON` names the whole key of the table it adds, every left row meets at most one partner.

```sql
SELECT ...
FROM trades AS t
JOIN securities AS s
  ON t.ticker = s.ticker
JOIN prices AS p
  ON t.ticker = p.ticker
 AND t.date = p.date;
```
screens.question: `trades` has 7 rows, and every trade has a company and a close. How many rows does the pattern return?

options.why: That is the count with only the ticker in the second `ON`. Here it names the whole key.
That is every trade with every company. The first `ON` keeps only matching tickers.
That is $7 \times 6 \times 18$, every combination. Each `ON` keeps only the matching rows.

feedback.correct: One row per trade: a full-key join never multiplies rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many partners does each `ON` allow?

explain.text: Each `ON` names a whole primary key, so each trade meets one company and one close. The result keeps one row per trade: 7.

Join `prices` with `ON p.ticker = t.ticker` `AND p.date = '2026-03-04'`.
Join `securities` for the sector, then `GROUP BY s.sector` and `ORDER BY s.sector`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your first row with the example.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 changes an old Barclays close, which exposure should ignore. Value every trade at the 2026-03-04 close.

explain.text: Barclays nets 1,000 − 400 = 600 shares at £2.51, and HSBC 600 at £8.69: Banks £6,720.00. Fixing the date in `ON` still names the whole key, so each trade meets one close. Taking the trade's own date instead would give trade values, not today's exposure.

ideas: `JOIN ... ON` pairs each left row with every right row where `ON` is true. An inner join keeps only those pairs.
Name the right table's whole key in `ON`: `t.ticker = p.ticker AND t.date = p.date`. Half a key or no `ON` multiplies rows.
An index on the join key lets SQLite `SEARCH` instead of `SCAN`, so each lookup reads only the matching rows.

formula.name: Rows from a join
formula.tex: \text{rows} = \sum_{\text{left rows}} (\text{right rows where ON is true})
formula.note: With no `ON` every term is the full right table: $7 \times 6 = 42$.

summary.trap: A join without `ON`, or on half a key, runs without error and quietly multiplies rows and totals.

quiz.prose:
`trades` has 7 rows and `prices` has 18.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM trades, prices;
```
quiz.question: How many rows does it return?

feedback.correct: A comma with no condition is a cross join: $7 \times 18$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no condition, which pairs are kept?

byKey.sum: You added the counts. Every trade pairs with every price, so they multiply.
byKey.seven: You expected one price per trade. Nothing here says which price goes with which trade.
byKey.eighteen: Each of the 18 prices pairs with all 7 trades, not just one.

explain.text: Listing two tables with a comma and no `WHERE` keeps every pair: $7 \times 18 = 126$ rows. It is the same cross join as `JOIN` without `ON`.

quiz.prose: A P&L report joins 40 trades to a `prices` table holding 5 days per ticker, with `ON t.ticker = p.ticker` only. It then sums `qty * close`.
quiz.question: How does the result compare with the right total?

options.text: It sums 200 rows, each trade once per close
It is correct: SQL picks the matching close
options.why: You expected SQL to find the right day. With only the ticker in `ON`, each trade meets all five closes.

options.text: It sums 40 rows but at the wrong closes
options.why: The join does not choose one close per trade. Each trade appears five times.

options.text: SQLite raises an error for the duplicate rows
options.why: Duplicate rows are legal in a result. The query runs and the number is wrong.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many closes does each trade meet?

explain.text: Half the key lets each trade meet all five closes, so 40 trades become 200 rows. The total mixes five days of prices and is roughly five times too large.

quiz.prose:
Someone joins on the wrong column:

```sql
SELECT t.id
FROM trades AS t
JOIN securities AS s
  ON t.ticker = s.name;
```

Use this lesson's tables.
quiz.question: How many rows does it return?

widget.label: Rows returned
widget.accept: 1: only trade 5, because BP's name equals its ticker.

feedback.correct: Only BP, whose name is also BP.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each traded ticker with every company name.

byKey.zero: Almost. Look at BP: its name and its ticker are both BP.
byKey.seven: A ticker such as BARC never equals a name such as Barclays, so most trades find nothing.

explain.text: A ticker equals a name only for BP, so only trade 5 survives. A wrong-column join often returns a few plausible rows, which makes it harder to spot than an empty result.

quiz.prose:
`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for a join prints two lines:

```text
SCAN t
SEARCH p USING INDEX idx_ticker (ticker=?)
```
quiz.question: What does SQLite do?

options.text: Scans the trades, then searches prices for each
Reads every row of both tables
options.why: Only `SCAN` reads a whole table. `SEARCH` jumps to matching rows.

options.text: Uses an index on both tables
options.why: Only `p` is searched through an index. `t` is scanned.

options.text: Reads every price, then looks up each trade
options.why: The scan is on `t`, the trades. The prices are the side that is searched.

feedback.correct: One scan of trades, one index lookup per trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which table is scanned, and which searched?

explain.text: `SCAN t` reads the trades once. For each trade, `SEARCH p USING INDEX` jumps to the prices with that ticker.
